evaluation.positioning_hook: A disgraced San Francisco engineer starts receiving capsules from his future self, only to discover his own survival depends on outsmarting a tech mogul who’s using time to turn rivals into targets.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and commercially sticky: a fallen tech genius, a mysterious device, and a race against a future conspiracy. It has broad genre appeal, though the tech-world specificity and darker moral turn keep it a notch below four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands in the opening pages with Park’s murder-suicide, the capsule disintegrating, and then Elliot waking up to the first hologram from his future self. The script is built around a clean, explainable engine: messages from the future are steering present-day choices.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Elliot is a strong lead because he’s brilliant, self-destructive, funny, and emotionally compromised by Robyn and his own failure. Craig, Robyn, Wilkes, and Prescott all have sharp enough edges to matter, though Elliot remains the clear center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script fuses time-travel mechanics with startup culture, workplace humiliation, and a self-fulfilling assassination loop in a way that feels fresh. The boldest choice is making the future self both mentor and manipulator, which gives the concept a nasty, memorable twist.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: It moves with real urgency once the capsules start arriving, and each new reveal escalates the danger rather than resetting it. The back half is especially strong because the story keeps converting information into immediate physical jeopardy.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea is novel but easy to grasp: a man is being coached by his future self into a chain of actions that may be saving him or destroying him. That combination of clean premise and escalating paranoia is the script’s most marketable originality.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The tech-company ecosystem, Silicon Valley vanity, and San Francisco geography give the story a specific social texture. It’s not a sprawling world, but the corporate hierarchy, startup culture, and future-tech rules generate enough story pressure to feel lived-in.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is a sharp blend of sardonic, anxious, and sleekly genre-forward, with jokes landing inside genuinely dangerous situations. The script has a confident voice that can pivot from hangdog comedy to hard-edged thriller without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s real thematic depth in the idea that self-belief, memory, and fate can become weapons, and the Robyn/Elliot material gives the story emotional residue. The script is still primarily a high-concept thriller, but it suggests more beneath the surface than the premise alone.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Elliot/Robyn is the emotional spine, and Craig/Wilkes/Prescott create a strong triangle of rivalry and betrayal around him. It’s not an ensemble piece, but the relationships are active enough that scenes keep generating tension beyond the central plot mechanics.

lead_characters.name: Elliot Lockhart
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, Korean-American, tech engineer / inventor, emotionally volatile, urban professional
lead_characters.hook: A once-brilliant inventor now living in the wreckage of a public failure, Elliot is funny, self-lacerating, and deeply allergic to his own potential. He’s the kind of man who can reverse-engineer time capsules in his apartment but still can’t trust his gut, and the script makes that contradiction the engine of the whole story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Ryan Gosling in Drive or Jake Gyllenhaal in Nightcrawler: a damaged, highly watchable lead who can play charm, shame, panic, and intelligence in the same scene. The role gives an actor a full-spectrum arc from washed-up loser to dangerous believer, with big emotional turns and plenty of dry comic bite.

lead_characters.name: Robyn Gilmore
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Elliot’s ex, nurse, emotionally intelligent, grounded
lead_characters.hook: Robyn is the one person who can see through Elliot’s performance and still choose to help him. She’s practical under pressure, emotionally wounded but not sentimental, and the script smartly uses her as both the audience’s reality check and Elliot’s last real tether to a life he blew up.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded authority of Emily Blunt in Edge of Tomorrow or Rebecca Ferguson in Mission: Impossible—smart, capable, and emotionally legible without ever becoming passive. She gets sharp dialogue, crisis competence, and the rare chance to be the person who can match the lead beat for beat.

lead_characters.name: Craig Bollinger
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, Elliot’s best friend, successful tech operator, charismatic, affluent
lead_characters.hook: Craig is the guy who looks like he won the game Elliot lost, and the script uses that status gap to make him both comic relief and a genuine threat. He’s affable, smug, and emotionally slippery, which makes his betrayal land with real force.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the polished-bro charm of Bradley Cooper in Limitless or Jon Hamm in a prestige ensemble—easy charisma with a darker undertow. The eventual turn into menace gives the part more bite than a standard best-friend foil.

lead_characters.name: Jonathan Wilkes
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-60s, tech mogul, polished, charismatic, predatory
lead_characters.hook: Wilkes is the script’s sleek corporate villain: a visionary who talks like a futurist and behaves like a war criminal with a product launch. He’s magnetic enough to sell the room and cold enough to justify the story’s darkest turns.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is premium antagonist material in the lane of Michael Keaton in Spider-Man: Homecoming or Jeremy Irons in Margin Call—controlled, witty, and dangerous. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing intelligence as menace, with a late-script reveal that reframes everything.

lead_characters.name: David Prescott
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, Elliot’s boss and later rival, ambitious, petty, corporate
lead_characters.hook: Prescott is the small-minded operator who mistakes authority for destiny, and the script keeps him sharp enough to matter without overcomplicating him. He’s the kind of antagonist whose resentment feels personal, which makes his future self’s involvement especially nasty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great character-actor role in the mold of Paul Dano in There Will Be Blood or Shea Whigham in a prestige thriller: a man whose insecurity curdles into danger. The stairwell confrontation and later reveal give the actor a strong escalation path.

lead_characters.name: Maguire
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, hired gun, working-class, Irish, professional killer
lead_characters.hook: Maguire is the script’s most unnerving pure function: a calm, methodical killer who treats murder like a shift job. He’s not flashy, which is exactly why he works; he feels like a man who has made peace with being a tool.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the dead-eyed menace of Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom or Michael Shannon in a low-key thriller. The part is compact but memorable, with a cool, controlled surface that makes the violence hit harder.

lead_characters.name: Harold
lead_characters.hook: Harold is the quiet institutional ghost who knows how the building works and, more importantly, knows how people work. He’s warm, wry, and unexpectedly loyal, giving the story a human anchor inside the corporate machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that can become a scene-stealer in the vein of John Goodman in a prestige thriller: brief, grounded, and memorable. It gives an older actor a chance to play dignity and mischief without exposition overload.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a Korean or Korean-American actor in his 30s
Robyn requires a strong grounded female supporting lead
Wilkes and Maguire are both actor-forward villain roles
Several roles are age-flexible but need strong comic timing and intensity

notable_requirements: San Francisco and Bay Area urban settings

technical.vfx_details: Hologram projections, capsule materialization/disintegration, time-travel visual effects, and a few stylized energy/flicker moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, practical blood effects, fire/explosion sequence in the lab, car chase/crash beats, and practical electrical effects.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with strong streamer and specialty theatrical upside

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior-driven, but the museum chase, multiple car beats, mansion break-in, fire-heavy lab climax, and repeated VFX capsule work keep this above a simple contained-thriller spend.

casting.note: The lead is a specific Korean-American 30s role that needs both comic timing and wounded intensity, and Wilkes/Maguire each need actor-grade menace to land cleanly.

development.note: The time-loop logic is clear enough to track, but the script asks the audience to absorb a lot of causal machinery while the story is still moving at thriller speed.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the high-concept time-loop urgency and the pressure of a protagonist trying to solve a mystery before the next reset.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, high-concept thrillers with emotional stakes and a tech-world edge.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but viable for women via the Robyn relationship and the romantic undercurrent; educated, urban, streamer-friendly audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, a moderate VFX load, several action beats, and a contained but not minimal cast keep it in the upper indie range.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of smart, adult sci-fi with a clean hook and enough emotional weight to travel beyond genre-only buyers. The script’s mix of paranoia, romance, and corporate conspiracy makes it attractive to buyers looking for concept plus character.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed central arc; the capsule mythology is strong, but no clear spinoff vector emerges beyond this story.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a fast, buyer-friendly pitch that can be understood in one breath and sold on premise alone. That makes it attractive to streamer dev execs and genre financiers who need a clean hook before they commit to a read.
strengths.evidence: The script opens with Park’s murder-suicide, the capsule disintegrating, and then Elliot discovering the first future-self hologram.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Elliot is a strong antihero lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role can carry the movie because it combines intelligence, self-loathing, humor, and romantic damage in a way that feels castable and playable. That’s the kind of part that can elevate a mid-budget thriller into actor-driven prestige territory.
strengths.evidence: Elliot’s self-deprecating banter, his relapse into drinking, and his repeated failure to trust his own instincts all define him on the page.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The future-self mechanic has a nasty twist.
strengths.what_it_means: The time-travel device isn’t just a gimmick; it becomes a moral trap, which gives the concept real staying power. Buyers respond to that because it turns a clean sci-fi hook into a paranoia engine with escalating consequences.
strengths.evidence: Future Elliot first helps, then steers him toward actions that reveal a larger conspiracy and a possible murder chain.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Robyn relationship adds emotional ballast.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the movie a human center that broadens the audience beyond pure genre fans and gives the lead a real emotional objective. It also helps the script play to buyers who want elevated genre with relationship stakes.
strengths.evidence: Robyn’s late-night confrontation, her decision to help him, and the motel surgery sequence all deepen the bond.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The corporate conspiracy is cleanly scalable.
strengths.what_it_means: The story’s villain structure is easy to package because it maps onto recognizable power dynamics: failed inventor versus visionary mogul. That’s useful for marketing and for attaching actors who want a clear antagonist with stature.
strengths.evidence: Wilkes’ reveal as the architect of the capsule scheme reframes the entire story and gives the climax a strong face.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has real set-piece momentum.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie keeps converting exposition into action, which is exactly what a producer wants in a high-concept thriller. That makes it easier to sell as a propulsive feature rather than a talky sci-fi idea.
strengths.evidence: The motel chase, stairwell fight, post office shootout, and lab fire sequence all escalate the stakes visually.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept sci-fi thriller with a real actor role at the center and a premium-streaming-friendly premise that sells in one sentence. The script pairs a contained, producible contemporary footprint with a strong emotional engine and a villain reveal that turns the whole movie into a race against time and self-destruction.

items.area: The premise depends on dense time mechanics.
items.detail: The capsule rules, memory-tracking logic, and future/past causality all need the audience to stay oriented while the story is moving fast. That’s not a deal-breaker, but it does make the buy somewhat conditional on the buyer’s appetite for concept-forward exposition.

Elliot is written as a Korean-American man in his 30s, and the part needs someone who can play wounded comedy, technical intelligence, and escalating paranoia without flattening any one lane. That’s a strong role, but it is a specific one.

items.area: The climax leans on fire and VFX.
items.detail: The Wilkes lab sequence requires practical fire, heavy smoke, electrical failure, and a weaponized capsule effect that has to read clearly on screen. It’s still in indie range, but this is the part of the movie most likely to push production planning.

items.area: Several brand references need a legal pass.
items.detail: The script names Altria, Aston Martin, Hugo Boss, iPad, Rohypnol, Wired, Sony, Apple, NASA, and Fats Domino, so clearance work is not trivial. Most are manageable, but the prominence of the brands means business affairs will want a careful review.

items.area: The movie is strongest when it’s moving.
items.detail: The early setup and later conspiracy reveal are strong, but the script’s appeal is most obvious once the capsules start driving immediate danger. Buyers will notice that the concept’s commercial lift is tied to momentum, not just premise.

issues.headline: The main friction is conceptual density: the script asks the audience to track a lot of time-travel logic while also following a betrayal-heavy thriller. Add a specific lead-casting lane and a handful of brand clearances, and this becomes a smart buy that still needs disciplined packaging.
